A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARSQ research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original ARSQ experiments on D4RL and RLBench, component ablations, temperature sensitivity, and computational measurements. Some baseline results are explicitly attributed to earlier work.

after.justification: v2 retains original ARSQ results and adds fully offline and fully online evaluations, reevaluated DWBC results, and a controlled Q-prediction error study.

M1.justification: The written method specification is corrected: Equation (16) adds the temperature multiplier to log-sum-exp normalization, and Equation (18) squares the training residual. The architecture, conditioning scheme, and algorithms remain substantively unchanged. These formula corrections do not establish that the implementation changed.

E1.justification: The same nine D4RL dataset/task combinations and 20 RLBench tasks remain. Appendix G adds a five-mode synthetic reward landscape beyond the original three-mode motivating example. Fully offline and demonstration-free online evaluations broaden data-access conditions on retained locomotion tasks, without adding another application domain.

E2.justification: The new offline comparison includes CQL, IQL, TD3+BC, Onestep RL, RvS-R, filtered BC, Decision Transformer, and DWBC. Most comparator scores come from cited papers, with selected DWBC results reevaluated. Appendix F also adds PPO to the online comparison. Existing main-experiment comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix F introduce fully offline and fully online training protocols. Offline ARSQ and reevaluated DWBC use 10 evaluation trajectories; DWBC labels the top 5% of trajectories as expert. Appendix G introduces 2,000 training points and 1,000 error-evaluation points. Newly specified tasks for existing ablations are disclosures, not established protocol changes.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds a controlled analysis of Q-prediction and discretization errors, comparing independent decomposition, ARSQ without coarse-to-fine discretization, and full ARSQ. New D4RL learning curves examine convergence, while Appendix F compares learning with different data-access regimes. The earlier conditioning, backbone, and temperature analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports three seeds for existing demonstration-quality, RLBench, ablation, and sensitivity experiments, beyond v1's main D4RL disclosure. It adds error bars to previously unaccompanied auxiliary results and reports uncertainty in new tables. This establishes expanded reporting, not an increase in runs; uncertainty conventions remain unspecified.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports an offline aggregate score of 741.1 for ARSQ versus 698.5 for CQL; Table 4 reports Q errors of 17.57, 0.50, and 0.16 for independent decomposition, ARSQ without coarse-to-fine discretization, and ARSQ. Online and convergence results are added. Existing Figure 5 revises bottom-30% ARSQ/CQN scores from 73.1/33.8 to 69.8/35.7, reducing the stated ratio from 2.2 to 2.0. Ablation and sensitivity values also change; Figure 4's headline results remain.

T1.justification: The added temperature multiplier in Equation (16) repairs the mathematical normalization needed to satisfy the dimensional-advantage constraint. Theorem 4.3 and its Appendix A proof remain substantively unchanged; rewriting log-sum-exp equal to zero as an exponential sum equal to one is equivalent.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about dimensional soft advantages, autoregressive action dependencies, and learning from suboptimal data. The headline 1.62-fold D4RL comparison is unchanged; added experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: Appendix G newly attributes prediction glitches without coarse-to-fine discretization to inadequate coverage of numerous action bins. Appendix F distinguishes demonstrations' benefit to learning speed from online interaction's benefit to final performance. The existing inference-latency limitation and proposed future remedies remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page URL, identifies datasets used for existing ablations and sensitivity tests, and documents DrQ-v2+'s critic, exploration, and configuration differences. Existing hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain. Conversely, Appendix C.3 removes v1's explicit statement that the RLBench baseline scores were taken from the CQN paper.

R1.justification: References and comparisons are added for offline methods including IQL, TD3+BC, Onestep RL, Decision Transformer, RvS, and DWBC. The central related-work discussion and positioning relative to CQN and autoregressive Q-learning remain stable. Numerous other reference changes are publication-metadata updates rather than new cited works.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify dimensional advantages, double value networks, and DrQ-v2+. A fully offline subsection and Appendices F–G extend the existing structure, while most original prose and organization remain. Affiliations, proceedings information, acknowledgements, and heading capitalization are also updated.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with offline-performance and Q-error tables, D4RL and online learning curves, and Q-landscape/error heatmaps. Existing diagrams and plots are redrawn or rescaled, with revised legends and appendix placement. The original demonstration-quality and 20-task RLBench figures are retained and renumbered, not newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects important normalization and loss-specification errors and substantially strengthens empirical justification through offline/online evaluations and a controlled test of the proposed discretization mechanism. Broader seed disclosures and uncertainty reporting also improve assessability. These gains concern correctness and evidential support, not higher headline performance, which remains unchanged. Removing explicit RLBench baseline-score provenance and leaving uncertainty conventions undefined are drawbacks, but they do not outweigh the substantive improvements.
